title: Business
levelNote: Six tiers in one file. The same topic from office and email up to shareholder, merger and quarterly forecast.

lines.text: Hi, I'm Ana. I'm the new manager.
Nice to meet you, Ana. I'm Pedro.
Nice to meet you too. Where is my office?
It's next to mine, on the second floor.
Great. Do we have a meeting today?
Yes, at ten o'clock, in the small room.
Are you free on Thursday afternoon?
I have a meeting until three. After that, I'm free.
Good. Let's talk about the budget then.
Should we invite the client too?
Not this time. Just our department.
Okay. I'll check the schedule and send an invite.
Thanks. Can we also look at the deadline for the report?

Sure. I think the numbers were strong.
They were. Revenue was up, and two new clients signed contracts.
I worked hard on that presentation for the second client.
It showed. I would like you to lead the negotiation with the next stakeholder.
I would be glad to. What about the budget for the project?
That has not been decided yet. I will let you know by Friday.
Sounds good. Thank you for the opportunity.

reading.title: The new office
reading.text:
Sofia started her new job on Monday. Her office was small, but it had a big window. She liked it right away.

At nine o'clock, she met her manager and three colleagues. They had a short meeting and talked about her first week. Everyone was friendly, and Sofia felt welcome.

At the end of the day, she sent an email to her family. "I love my new job," she wrote.

questions.q: Who did Sofia meet at nine o'clock?
What did Sofia do at the end of the day?
options: She sent an email to her family

reading.title: The empty inbox
reading.text:
Marco used to believe that answering every email quickly made him good at his job. For two years, his inbox was always empty by six o'clock, and he was proud of that.

Then he noticed something. The fastest replies were not always the most useful ones, and the projects that mattered most were the ones he had been too busy answering email to finish. His manager had said the same thing in his last review, but it had not made sense until now.

These days, Marco checks his email twice a day, not twenty times. His inbox is rarely empty, and his reports are better than they have ever been. He still gets nervous when he sees fifty unread messages, but he no longer believes that number means anything about his work.

questions.q: What was Marco proud of at first?
options: An empty inbox by six o'clock
His fastest replies were not always useful
His colleagues were slower than him

reading.title: The real cost of a meeting
reading.text:
A meeting with eight people for one hour does not cost one hour. It costs eight hours, taken from eight different jobs that were not being done during that time, and paid for at eight different salaries. Almost nobody calculates it this way, which is exactly why so many meetings that should have been an email still happen every day.

The habit is not really about communication. It is about certainty. A decision made alone can be blamed on one person, but a decision made in a room with everyone present feels shared, even when only two people in the room actually needed to be there. The meeting becomes a way of spreading responsibility rather than a way of making a better decision.

None of this means meetings are wasteful by nature. A negotiation, a difficult performance review, or a genuine disagreement about strategy needs people in a room, because tone and timing matter and an email cannot supply either. The real skill is not avoiding meetings altogether. It is asking, honestly, whether this particular decision needs eight people or one honest conversation with the two who actually disagree.

questions.q: Why does the writer say an eight-person meeting costs more than it seems?
options: It takes people away from eight different jobs

questions.q: What does the writer say meetings are really about, beyond communication?
What does the writer think is the real skill?
options: Asking whether a decision truly needs many people
